title: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters, using the sliding window pattern. Explain the approach, the data structures, the time and space complexity, and demonstrate it with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: No-repeat Substring (Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters)

s1_definition.profdef: The no-repeat substring problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous run of characters in a string where every character is distinct. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window: a right pointer expands the window one character at a time, and a hash map or index array remembers the most recent position of each character so that when a duplicate enters the window, the left pointer jumps forward past the previous occurrence. The algorithm runs in linear time because each character is visited at most twice.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a long tape of transaction-channel codes printed one after another, such as ATM, UPI, NEFT, ATM again, and so on. He wants the longest stretch where no channel repeats, because that represents the longest span of fully diverse channel usage. He slides a highlighter rightward over the tape, and the moment a channel he already highlighted shows up again, he lifts the left edge of the highlighter forward until the repeat is gone, always remembering the longest clean stretch he has seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right, and when a character repeats, jump left past its last position, tracking the longest distinct window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The no-repeat substring problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous run of characters in a string where every character is distinct. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window: a right pointer expands the window one character at a time, and a hash map or index array remembers the most recent position of each character so that when a duplicate enters the window, the left pointer jumps forward past the previous occurrence. The algorithm runs in linear time because each character is visited at most twice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a long tape of transaction-channel codes printed one after another, such as ATM, UPI, NEFT, ATM again, and so on. He wants the longest stretch where no channel repeats, because that represents the longest span of fully diverse channel usage. He slides a highlighter rightward over the tape, and the moment a channel he already highlighted shows up again, he lifts the left edge of the highlighter forward until the repeat is gone, always remembering the longest clean stretch he has seen.

**One line to remember:** Expand right, and when a character repeats, jump left past its last position, tracking the longest distinct window.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is to maintain a window described by two indices, a left boundary and a right boundary, such that the substring between them never contains a repeated character. We move the right boundary forward through the string one step at a time. For each new character we need to answer one question quickly: have we seen this character already inside the current window, and if so, where?

To answer that in constant time we keep a map from a character to the index of its most recent appearance. In Java this is often a `HashMap<Character, Integer>`, and for pure ASCII input an `int[128]` index array is faster. When the right pointer lands on a character, we look it up. If the stored index is greater than or equal to the current left boundary, the character is a duplicate that lives inside our window, so we move the left boundary to one position past that stored index. For example `int last = seen.getOrDefault(c, -1); if (last >= left) left = last + 1;` guarantees the window stays duplicate-free.

After adjusting the left boundary, we record the character's new position with `seen.put(c, right)` and then compute the current window length as `right - left + 1`, updating the best length with `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`. The crucial senior-level nuance is the condition `last >= left`. We must not blindly jump left backward when a stale index, belonging to a character that already fell out of the window, is found in the map; comparing against the current left boundary prevents the window from ever shrinking incorrectly.

The time complexity is linear, O(n), because the right pointer advances exactly n times and the left pointer only ever moves forward, so across the whole run the two pointers perform at most 2n moves. The space complexity is O(k) where k is the size of the character alphabet, which is bounded and effectively constant for ASCII. This two-pointer discipline, where neither pointer retreats, is the signature of the sliding window family and is why it beats the naive O(n squared) approach of checking every substring.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the fraud-analytics desk records, for each customer session, the ordered sequence of transaction-channel codes the customer touched, written as a single string of single-letter codes such as A for ATM, U for UPI, N for NEFT, I for IMPS, and C for card. Analysts want to measure the longest continuous stretch within a session in which the customer never reused a channel, because a long diverse-channel stretch is a strong behavioural fingerprint and a sudden collapse in that length between sessions can signal account takeover. This is exactly the no-repeat substring problem: the longest window with all distinct characters.

Problem 2 — Doing this the naive way, by testing every possible start and end position and checking each for duplicates, is far too slow for the millions of sessions the bank processes nightly. We need the linear sliding-window approach so the batch job finishes inside its window. This is where remembering each channel's last-seen position lets the left edge of the window leap forward instantly instead of rescanning.

The code will contain an `Account` class with the usual accountId, holderName and balance so the project ties into the same banking system, a `ChannelSequenceAnalyzer` service whose `longestDistinctChannelRun` method implements the sliding window, and a runnable `NoRepeatSubstringDemo` main class that feeds Rajesh's and Priya's session strings through the analyzer, logs each window adjustment at fine level, and logs the final longest clean run at info level. Every class is a normal top-level class, not a static inner class.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's session string "AUNICAUN", processed character by character with a last-seen map, a left boundary starting at 0, and a best length starting at 0.

Step 1: Right points at index 0, channel A. The map has no A, so no jump. We record A at 0. Window is index 0 to 0, length 1, so best becomes 1.

Step 2: Right moves to index 1, channel U. No previous U, record U at 1. Window 0 to 1, length 2, best becomes 2.

Step 3: Right at index 2, channel N. New channel, record N at 2. Window length 3, best becomes 3.

Step 4: Right at index 3, channel I. New, record I at 3. Window length 4, best becomes 4.

Step 5: Right at index 4, channel C. New, record C at 4. Window length 5, best becomes 5. This is the longest clean stretch "AUNIC".

Step 6: Right at index 5, channel A. The map says A was last at index 0, and 0 is greater than or equal to left 0, so A is a duplicate inside the window. We move left to 0 plus 1, which is 1, then record A at 5. Window is index 1 to 5, length 5, best stays 5.

Step 7: Right at index 6, channel U. Map says U was at index 1, and 1 is greater than or equal to left 1, so duplicate; move left to 2, record U at 6. Window 2 to 6, length 5, best stays 5.

Step 8: Right at index 7, channel N. Map says N was at index 2, and 2 is greater than or equal to left 2, so duplicate; move left to 3, record N at 7. Window 3 to 7, length 5, best stays 5.

The final longest distinct channel run for Rajesh is 5.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The no-repeat substring problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous substring that contains no repeated character, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window in linear time. I keep a left boundary, a right pointer that scans the string once, and a map from each character to the index where I last saw it. As the right pointer moves forward over each character, I check the map, and if that character was last seen at a position that is at or after my current left boundary, it is a duplicate living inside the window, so I move the left boundary to one position past that previous occurrence. After that adjustment I update the character's position in the map and record the current window length, keeping the maximum as my answer.

The single most important detail I always call out is the condition that the previous index must be greater than or equal to the current left boundary before I move left. Without that guard, a stale position belonging to a character that already fell out of the window would incorrectly drag the window backward, so comparing against the live left boundary is what keeps the algorithm correct. Because the right pointer advances n times and the left pointer only ever moves forward, the total work is linear, which is far better than the naive approach of checking every substring.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I applied this on the fraud-analytics desk. For each customer session we stored the ordered sequence of transaction-channel codes, and we measured the longest continuous stretch where no channel repeated, because that diverse-channel run is a stable behavioural fingerprint. A sudden drop in that length from one session to the next was one of our early signals of a possible account takeover, and the linear sliding window let the nightly batch process millions of sessions comfortably within its time window.

The senior-level point I make is that this is the canonical variable-size sliding window, and recognizing that family of problems lets me reuse one mental template across many differently worded questions. I also mention that for a fixed ASCII alphabet I would replace the hash map with a small integer index array to cut constant factors, which matters when the job runs over hundreds of millions of characters, and that the space is bounded by the alphabet size rather than the input length. Showing that I reason about both correctness guards and real throughput is what an interviewer is listening for.
